stimuli.text: Researchers investigated whether caffeine improves attention. They recruited 80 university students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition drank coffee containing 200 milligrams of caffeine. Participants in the other condition drank decaffeinated coffee that tasted the same. The researchers then recorded the number of targets that each participant correctly detected in a ten-minute computer task.

Researchers investigated whether a smiling expression makes cartoons seem funnier. They recruited 90 university students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition held a pen between their teeth, which produces a smile. Participants in the other condition held a pen between their lips, which prevents a smile. The researchers then recorded the rating from 1 to 10 that each participant gave to a set of cartoons. The results are shown in the table. The difference between the two groups had a p value of 0.41.

rows.group: The group that held the pen between the teeth
The group that held the pen between the lips

stimuli.text: Researchers collected data from 400 high school students. For each one, they recorded the average number of hours slept per night and grade point average. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.45.

Researchers collected data from 600 university students. For each one, they recorded conscientiousness score on a personality inventory and grade point average. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.35.

Researchers investigated whether spreading study sessions out improves long-term retention. They recruited 90 high school students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition studied a list of 40 words in six ten-minute sessions on six different days. Participants in the other condition studied the same list in a single sixty-minute session. The researchers then recorded the number of words out of 40 that each participant recalled on a test one month later.

Researchers investigated whether nausea after a new taste produces an aversion to that taste. They recruited 40 laboratory rats and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Rats in one condition drank sweetened water and were then given an injection that causes mild nausea. Rats in the other condition drank sweetened water and were then given a harmless salt-water injection. The researchers then recorded the volume in milliliters of sweetened water that each rat drank the next day.

Researchers investigated whether the wording of a question changes what witnesses remember. They recruited 100 adult volunteers who watched a film of a car accident and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition were asked how fast the cars were going when they smashed into each other. Participants in the other condition were asked how fast the cars were going when they contacted each other. The researchers then recorded the speed in kilometers per hour that each participant wrote down. The results are shown in the table. The difference between the two groups had a p value of 0.01.

rows.group: The group asked the question with the word 'smashed'
The group asked the question with the word 'contacted'

stimuli.text: Researchers investigated whether mindfulness meditation lowers stress. They recruited 84 office workers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition practiced mindfulness meditation for twenty minutes a day for eight weeks. Participants in the other condition listened to an audiobook for twenty minutes a day for eight weeks. The researchers then recorded the level of the stress hormone cortisol in a saliva sample from each participant.

Researchers investigated whether a night without sleep slows reaction time. They recruited 60 adult volunteers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition stayed awake all night in the laboratory. Participants in the other condition slept for eight hours in the laboratory. The researchers then recorded the average time in milliseconds that each participant took to press a button when a light appeared.

Researchers investigated whether keeping a gratitude journal raises well-being. They recruited 110 adult volunteers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition wrote down three things they were grateful for every night for a month. Participants in the other condition wrote down three things they had done every night for a month. The researchers then recorded each participant's rating of life satisfaction on a scale from 1 to 10 at the end of the month.

Researchers investigated whether an expected reward reduces children's later interest in drawing. They recruited 60 preschool children who enjoyed drawing and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Children in one condition were promised a certificate for drawing and received it. Children in the other condition drew with no reward mentioned. The researchers then recorded the number of minutes that each child chose to spend drawing during free time one week later.

Researchers collected data from 300 families. For each one, they recorded the warmth of parenting, as rated by observers and the child's self-esteem score. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.48.

Researchers investigated whether agreeing to a small request makes people more likely to agree to a large one. They recruited 120 homeowners and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Homeowners in one condition were first asked to sign a road-safety petition and two weeks later were asked to put a large sign in their garden. Homeowners in the other condition were only asked to put the large sign in their garden. The researchers then recorded the percentage of homeowners in each group who agreed to display the sign.

Researchers investigated whether the presence of other people slows the reporting of an emergency. They recruited 80 university students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition were filling in a form in a room with four other people when smoke began to enter the room. Participants in the other condition were filling in the form alone when smoke began to enter the room. The researchers then recorded the time in seconds before each participant left the room to report the smoke.
Researchers collected data from 450 adults. For each one, they recorded optimism score and the number of days of illness in a year. The correlation between the two measures was r = −0.30.

Researchers investigated whether guided hints help children learn to solve puzzles. They recruited 64 five-year-old children and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Children in one condition solved practice puzzles with hints from an adult that were gradually reduced. Children in the other condition solved the same practice puzzles alone. The researchers then recorded the number of new puzzles out of ten that each child later solved without help.
Researchers collected data from 250 adults. For each one, they recorded resting heart rate and self-rated anxiety. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.38.

Read the summary of a hypothetical study, then answer parts A to F.

**Introduction.** Researchers investigated whether a phone conversation reduces what drivers notice. They hypothesized that phone use would affect attention to the road.

**Participants.** The sample was 64 licensed drivers, recruited from one city. All participants gave informed consent, were told they could withdraw at any time, and were debriefed afterward. The plan was approved by an institutional review board.

**Method.** The participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition held a hands-free phone conversation while using a driving simulator. Participants in the other condition used the driving simulator without a phone. The researchers recorded the number of road signs out of 30 that each participant failed to notice.

**Results.** The group that talked on the phone: mean road signs missed (out of 30) = 11.4. The group that drove without a phone: mean road signs missed (out of 30) = 4.9. The difference was statistically significant (p = 0.01).

Use the three hypothetical sources to answer the question: **Do rewards increase motivation?**

**Source A.** In an experiment, 60 preschool children who liked drawing were randomly assigned to draw for a promised certificate or to draw with no reward. A week later, during free play, the rewarded children chose to draw for a mean of 6.5 minutes and the unrewarded children for 13.8 minutes (p = 0.01).

**Source B.** In a study of 200 call-center workers, half were randomly assigned to receive a bonus for each sale. Over a month, the bonus group made a mean of 41 sales and the comparison group a mean of 33 (p = 0.02). When the bonus ended, the bonus group's sales fell to a mean of 30.

**Source C.** A survey of 500 university students found that students who said they studied mainly because they found their subject interesting had higher grades and reported less burnout than students who said they studied mainly for grades or money (r = +0.40 between interest and grades).

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Cluster C?

options.text: A lasting, rigid pattern of behavior and inner experience that differs from cultural expectations and impairs functioning
options.why: That describes a personality disorder.

options.text: The group of personality disorders marked by odd or eccentric behavior: paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal
options.why: That describes Cluster A.

options.text: The group of personality disorders marked by dramatic, emotional or erratic behavior: antisocial, borderline, histrionic and narcissistic
options.why: That describes Cluster B.

options.text: The group of personality disorders marked by anxious or fearful behavior: avoidant, dependent and obsessive-compulsive
options.why: Correct. This is what Cluster C means.

questions.explanation: Cluster C is the group of personality disorders marked by anxious or fearful behavior: avoidant, dependent and obsessive-compulsive.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the second phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the body stays highly aroused to cope with a continuing stressor?

options.why: The exhaustion phase is the third phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the body's resources run out and illness becomes more likely.
Correct. The resistance phase is the second phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the body stays highly aroused to cope with a continuing stressor.
The general adaptation syndrome is Selye's three-phase description of the body's response to long-term stress: alarm, resistance and exhaustion.
The alarm reaction is the first phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the sympathetic nervous system is suddenly activated.

questions.explanation: The resistance phase is the second phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the body stays highly aroused to cope with a continuing stressor.

questions.stem: A scientist explains color vision by saying that the retina's cones come in three kinds, each most sensitive to one color. Which theory is this?

options.why: Dichromatism is a form of color vision deficiency in which one of the three types of cones does not work.
Correct. The trichromatic theory is the theory that the retina has three types of color receptors, sensitive to red, green and blue.
Prosopagnosia is the inability to recognize faces, even familiar ones, after brain damage.
Monochromatism is a rare form of color blindness in which a person sees only shades of gray.

questions.explanation: The trichromatic theory is the theory that the retina has three types of color receptors, sensitive to red, green and blue.

questions.stem: All of the subjects in this study were drawn from one group: 80 university students. What does this most limit?

options.text: Whether a cause-and-effect conclusion can be drawn
options.why: Random assignment, not the sample, allows the causal conclusion.

options.text: How far the findings can be generalized to other populations
options.why: Correct. A sample that does not represent the wider population limits generalizability.

options.text: Whether the dependent variable was operationally defined
options.why: The measure was clearly defined.

options.text: Whether the study had a control group
options.why: The study had a comparison condition.

questions.explanation: A sample that does not represent the wider population limits generalizability.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes bulimia nervosa?

options.text: The neurodevelopmental disorder marked by persistent difficulty in reading, writing or math despite normal intelligence
options.why: That describes a specific learning disorder.

options.text: The neurodevelopmental disorder marked by inattention, hyperactivity and impulsiveness
options.why: That describes attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.

options.text: The eating disorder in which a person binges on food and then makes up for it by vomiting, fasting or excessive exercise
options.why: Correct. This is what bulimia nervosa means.

options.text: The eating disorder in which a person restricts food to the point of being dangerously underweight, with an intense fear of gaining weight
options.why: That describes anorexia nervosa.

questions.explanation: Bulimia nervosa is the eating disorder in which a person binges on food and then makes up for it by vomiting, fasting or excessive exercise.

questions.stem: A researcher claims that dreams have no hidden meaning; the cortex simply builds a story out of random signals from the brainstem. Which theory is this?

options.why: Correct. The activation-synthesis theory is the theory that dreams are the brain's attempt to make sense of random neural activity during sleep.
Restoration is the repair of body and brain tissue that takes place during sleep.
The consolidation theory is the theory that dreaming helps sort and strengthen the day's memories.
Memory consolidation is the strengthening of memories that takes place during sleep.

questions.explanation: The activation-synthesis theory is the theory that dreams are the brain's attempt to make sense of random neural activity during sleep.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the research method in which a researcher manipulates a variable and randomly assigns participants, which allows conclusions about cause and effect?

options.why: Correct. An experiment is the research method in which a researcher manipulates a variable and randomly assigns participants, which allows conclusions about cause and effect.
A survey is the research method of collecting self-reported attitudes or behaviors from a sample by asking questions.
Falsifiability is the quality of a claim that it could be shown to be wrong by evidence.
Naturalistic observation is the research method of watching and recording behavior in its natural setting without interfering.

questions.explanation: An experiment is the research method in which a researcher manipulates a variable and randomly assigns participants, which allows conclusions about cause and effect.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language?

options.why: Syntax is the rules for ordering words into sentences.
Correct. A phoneme is the smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language.
Grammar is the whole system of rules in a language that lets people communicate.
Semantics is the rules by which we get meaning from words and sentences.

questions.explanation: A phoneme is the smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the linking of new information to existing knowledge and meaning to store it in long-term memory?

options.why: Highly superior autobiographical memory is the rare ability to recall almost every day of one's life in detail.
Maintenance rehearsal is the repeating of information over and over to keep it in short-term memory.
Autobiographical memory is the memory of the events of one's own life.
Correct. Elaborative rehearsal is the linking of new information to existing knowledge and meaning to store it in long-term memory.

questions.explanation: Elaborative rehearsal is the linking of new information to existing knowledge and meaning to store it in long-term memory.

questions.stem: Which statement about the results is best supported?

options.text: The study shows that the two conditions always give identical results
options.why: A non-significant result does not show that there is no effect at all.

options.text: The independent variable had a large effect
options.why: The averages are close and the difference is not significant.

options.text: The difference between the groups is not statistically significant, so it could easily be due to chance
options.why: Correct. A p value above 0.05 means a difference this size would often occur by chance alone.

options.text: The difference between the groups is statistically significant
options.why: A p value of 0.41 is far above 0.05.

questions.explanation: A p value above 0.05 means a difference this size would often occur by chance alone.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the wrinkled outer layer of the brain, which handles thinking, perception and voluntary movement?

options.why: The corpus callosum is the band of fibers that connects the two hemispheres of the brain.
The hippocampus is the structure that forms new explicit memories of facts and events.
The hypothalamus is the structure that regulates hunger, thirst, body temperature and sexual behavior and controls the pituitary gland.
Correct. The cerebral cortex is the wrinkled outer layer of the brain, which handles thinking, perception and voluntary movement.

questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex is the wrinkled outer layer of the brain, which handles thinking, perception and voluntary movement.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes nonmaleficence?

options.text: The ethical principle that psychologists must be honest and accurate
options.why: That describes integrity.

options.text: The ethical principle that psychologists must avoid doing harm
options.why: Correct. This is what nonmaleficence means.

options.text: The ethical principle that psychologists must be trustworthy and keep their professional promises
options.why: That describes fidelity.

options.text: The ethical principle that psychologists must protect privacy, confidentiality and the right of people to make their own choices
options.why: That describes respect for people's rights and dignity.

questions.explanation: Nonmaleficence is the ethical principle that psychologists must avoid doing harm.

questions.stem: What does the correlation show?

options.text: The first measure causes the second
options.why: A correlation does not show cause and effect.

options.text: Higher values of the first measure tend to go with higher values of the second
options.why: Correct. A positive correlation means the two measures tend to move in the same direction.
A correlation of zero would show no relationship.

options.text: Higher values of the first measure tend to go with lower values of the second
options.why: That would be a negative correlation.

questions.explanation: A positive correlation means the two measures tend to move in the same direction.

questions.stem: What does the correlation show?

options.text: Higher values of the first measure tend to go with higher values of the second
options.why: Correct. A positive correlation means the two measures tend to move in the same direction.

options.text: The first measure causes the second
options.why: A correlation does not show cause and effect.

options.text: Higher values of the first measure tend to go with lower values of the second
options.why: That would be a negative correlation.
A correlation of zero would show no relationship.

questions.explanation: A positive correlation means the two measures tend to move in the same direction.

questions.stem: Another research team repeats this study with new subjects and obtains the same result. What is this called?

options.why: That is explaining the study to participants afterward.
Correct. Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.
That is how subjects are placed in conditions.
That is an in-depth study of one individual.

questions.explanation: Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be a confounding variable in this study?

options.text: The two groups differed in preference for sweetened water at the end of the study
options.why: That is the dependent variable, the result being measured.

options.text: Each one was assigned to a condition at random
options.why: Random assignment reduces confounding; it is not a confound.

options.text: The rats given the nausea-causing injection were several months older
options.why: Correct. It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

options.text: One group differed from the other in the type of injection given after drinking
options.why: That is the independent variable itself.

questions.explanation: It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

questions.stem: Red light and blue light differ in color. Which property of the light waves differs?

options.why: Frequency is the number of sound waves per second, which determines pitch.
Amplitude is the height of a sound wave, which determines loudness.
The cochlea is the coiled, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear where sound waves become neural impulses.
Correct. Wavelength is the distance from one wave peak to the next, which determines the hue of light.

questions.explanation: Wavelength is the distance from one wave peak to the next, which determines the hue of light.

questions.stem: A doctor prescribes a drug that blocks dopamine receptors to reduce a patient's hallucinations. Which kind of drug is this?

options.why: Tardive dyskinesia is the involuntary movements of the face and tongue that can result from long-term use of antipsychotic drugs.
Correct. An antipsychotic drug is a drug that reduces hallucinations and delusions by blocking dopamine receptors.
An antianxiety drug is a drug that reduces tension by depressing central nervous system activity and can be addictive.
An antidepressant is a drug, such as an SSRI, that treats depression and anxiety by raising the availability of serotonin or norepinephrine.

questions.explanation: An antipsychotic drug is a drug that reduces hallucinations and delusions by blocking dopamine receptors.

questions.stem: Which statement about the results is best supported?

options.text: The difference between the groups is statistically significant, so it is unlikely to be due to chance
options.why: Correct. A p value below 0.05 means a difference this large would rarely occur by chance alone.

options.text: The results prove that every individual in the first group differed from every individual in the second
options.why: The table reports group averages, not individual scores.

options.text: The difference between the groups is probably due to chance
options.why: A p value of 0.01 is below 0.05, so chance is an unlikely explanation.

options.text: The two groups had the same average result
options.why: The table shows different averages.

questions.explanation: A p value below 0.05 means a difference this large would rarely occur by chance alone.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be a confounding variable in this study?

options.text: The two groups differed in stress at the end of the study
options.why: That is the dependent variable, the result being measured.

options.text: The meditation group was moved to a quieter office during the study
options.why: Correct. It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

options.text: One group differed from the other in the daily activity
options.why: That is the independent variable itself.

options.text: Each one was assigned to a condition at random
options.why: Random assignment reduces confounding; it is not a confound.

questions.explanation: It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as Erikson's stage in young adulthood, in which people seek close, lasting relationships?

options.why: Generativity versus stagnation is Erikson's stage in middle adulthood, in which people seek to contribute to the world through family and work.
Identity versus role confusion is Erikson's stage in adolescence, in which teenagers work out who they are.
Integrity versus despair is Erikson's stage in late adulthood, in which people look back on life with satisfaction or regret.
Correct. Intimacy versus isolation is Erikson's stage in young adulthood, in which people seek close, lasting relationships.

questions.explanation: Intimacy versus isolation is Erikson's stage in young adulthood, in which people seek close, lasting relationships.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes disorganized attachment?

options.text: The comfort from physical touch that Harlow showed is more important to attachment than feeding
options.why: That describes contact comfort.

options.text: The insecure attachment style in which a child is very upset by separation and is not easily comforted on reunion
options.why: That describes anxious attachment.

options.text: The insecure attachment style in which a child shows confused, contradictory behavior toward the caregiver
options.why: Correct. This is what disorganized attachment means.

options.text: The distress that infants show when a familiar caregiver leaves, which peaks around 13 months
options.why: That describes separation anxiety.

questions.explanation: Disorganized attachment is the insecure attachment style in which a child shows confused, contradictory behavior toward the caregiver.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the extent to which the findings of a study apply to people beyond the sample?

options.why: A convenience sample is a sample made up of whoever is easiest for the researcher to reach.
Sampling bias is a flaw in selecting participants that makes the sample unlike the population.
Correct. Generalizability is the extent to which the findings of a study apply to people beyond the sample.
Random assignment is the placing of participants in experimental conditions by chance.

questions.explanation: Generalizability is the extent to which the findings of a study apply to people beyond the sample.

questions.stem: After being shouted at by her boss, Gia goes home and shouts at her younger brother. Which defense mechanism is this?

options.why: Rationalization is the defense mechanism of giving a comfortable excuse in place of the real reason for a behavior.
Projection is the defense mechanism of seeing one's own unacceptable impulses in other people.
Correct. Displacement is the defense mechanism of shifting an impulse from its real target to a safer one.
Denial is the defense mechanism of refusing to accept a painful reality.

questions.explanation: Displacement is the defense mechanism of shifting an impulse from its real target to a safer one.

questions.stem: A psychologist says rates of eating disorders are higher where the culture promotes an extremely thin body ideal. Which perspective is this?

options.why: The cognitive perspective is the view that disorders result from distorted or irrational ways of thinking.
The biological perspective is the view that disorders result from genetic, brain or chemical causes.
The humanistic perspective is the view that disorders result from blocked personal growth and a lack of acceptance.
Correct. The sociocultural perspective is the view that disorders result from social and cultural factors, such as poverty and discrimination.

questions.explanation: The sociocultural perspective is the view that disorders result from social and cultural factors, such as poverty and discrimination.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a token economy?

options.text: The behavioral treatment that pairs an unwanted behavior with an unpleasant stimulus
options.why: That describes aversion therapy.

options.text: The behavioral system in which people earn tokens for desired behavior and exchange them for rewards
options.why: Correct. This is what a token economy means.

options.text: The exposure therapy that pairs relaxation with a graded series of anxiety-arousing stimuli
options.why: That describes systematic desensitization.

options.text: The technique of using electronic monitoring to show a person their body's signals so that they can learn to control them
options.why: That describes biofeedback.

questions.explanation: A token economy is the behavioral system in which people earn tokens for desired behavior and exchange them for rewards.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the extent to which test scores forecast the future performance they are meant to predict?

options.why: Standardization is the giving and scoring of a test in the same way for everyone, and the comparison of scores with a pretested group.
Correct. Predictive validity is the extent to which test scores forecast the future performance they are meant to predict.
Split-half reliability is the consistency of scores between two halves of the same test.
Construct validity is the extent to which a test measures the concept it claims to measure.

questions.explanation: Predictive validity is the extent to which test scores forecast the future performance they are meant to predict.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes retroactive interference?

options.text: In psychodynamic theory, the pushing of anxiety-arousing memories out of awareness
options.why: That describes repression.

options.text: The disruption of older memories by new learning
options.why: Correct. This is what retroactive interference means.

options.text: The disruption of new learning by older memories
options.why: That describes proactive interference.

options.text: The pattern in which memory fades quickly at first and then levels off
options.why: That describes the forgetting curve.

questions.explanation: Retroactive interference is the disruption of older memories by new learning.

questions.stem: Gus must either clean the bathroom or wash the dishes, and he hates both. Which kind of conflict is this?

options.why: Correct. An avoidance-avoidance conflict is a conflict in which a person must choose between two unattractive options.
An approach-approach conflict is a conflict in which a person must choose between two attractive options.
Intrinsic motivation is the desire to do something for its own sake, because it is enjoyable or satisfying.
Extrinsic motivation is the desire to do something to gain a reward or avoid a punishment.

questions.explanation: An avoidance-avoidance conflict is a conflict in which a person must choose between two unattractive options.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as a mental picture of the layout of one's surroundings?

options.why: Latent learning is learning that takes place without reinforcement and is not shown until there is a reason to show it.
Vicarious conditioning is learning from seeing the consequences of another person's behavior.
Observational learning is learning by watching others and imitating them.
Correct. A cognitive map is a mental picture of the layout of one's surroundings.

questions.explanation: A cognitive map is a mental picture of the layout of one's surroundings.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the perception that an object keeps the same color under different lighting?

options.why: Shape constancy is the perception that an object keeps the same shape even when the viewing angle changes.
Apparent movement is the perception of motion when a series of still images or lights is shown in quick succession.
Correct. Color constancy is the perception that an object keeps the same color under different lighting.
Size constancy is the perception that an object keeps the same size even when its image on the retina changes.

questions.explanation: Color constancy is the perception that an object keeps the same color under different lighting.

questions.stem: In the 1940s, surgeons cut the connections to patients' frontal lobes to calm them, often leaving them permanently listless. Which procedure was this?

options.why: Psychotropic medication is any drug that acts on the brain to treat the symptoms of a psychological disorder.
Correct. A lobotomy is the now-abandoned form of psychosurgery that cut the nerves connecting the frontal lobes to the rest of the brain.
Electroconvulsive therapy is the treatment for severe depression in which a brief electric current is passed through the brain of an anesthetized patient.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation is the treatment in which repeated magnetic pulses are applied to the surface of the brain to treat depression.

questions.explanation: A lobotomy is the now-abandoned form of psychosurgery that cut the nerves connecting the frontal lobes to the rest of the brain.

questions.stem: After losing his home in a flood, Jay copes, rebuilds and returns to his normal level of functioning. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Signature strengths is the positive character traits, such as kindness or curiosity, that are most central to a particular person.
Correct. Resilience is the ability to recover and adapt well after stress or hardship.
Positive psychology is the scientific study of the strengths and conditions that help people and communities thrive.
Posttraumatic growth is the positive psychological change that some people experience after struggling with a very difficult event.

questions.explanation: Resilience is the ability to recover and adapt well after stress or hardship.

questions.stem: In a drug trial, half of the patients receive the new medication. This half is which of the following?

options.why: A placebo is an inactive substance or treatment that looks like the real one.
A single-blind procedure is a procedure in which the participants do not know which condition they are in.
Correct. The experimental group is the group in an experiment that receives the treatment being tested.
Statistical significance is the conclusion that a result is unlikely to have occurred by chance, usually when p is below 0.05.

questions.explanation: The experimental group is the group in an experiment that receives the treatment being tested.

questions.stem: After the study, the researchers explained its full purpose to every participant and answered their questions. What is this called?

options.why: Correct. Debriefing explains the study, including any deception, once it is over.
A placebo is an inactive treatment.
Replication is repeating a study.
Consent is obtained before the study.

questions.explanation: Debriefing explains the study, including any deception, once it is over.

questions.stem: At two months, a baby makes soft 'ooh' and 'aah' sounds. Which stage of language development is this?

options.why: Babbling is the stage from about four months in which infants produce many consonant-vowel sounds, such as 'ba-ba'.
Overgeneralization is the applying of a grammar rule too widely, as in 'goed' or 'mouses'.
Correct. Cooing is the vowel-like sounds, such as 'ooh', that infants make from about two months.
Telegraphic speech is the two-word stage in which a child uses mostly nouns and verbs, such as 'want juice'.

questions.explanation: Cooing is the vowel-like sounds, such as 'ooh', that infants make from about two months.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the operational definition of the dependent variable?

options.text: Each participant's rating of life satisfaction on a scale from 1 to 10 at the end of the month
options.why: Correct. An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

options.text: The random assignment of each one to a condition
options.why: This is a control procedure, not a definition of a variable.
This is the independent variable.
This names the variable but does not say how it was measured.

questions.explanation: An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

questions.stem: A child grows up in a society that places a high value on respect for elders. In ecological systems theory, this cultural value is part of which system?

options.why: Correct. The macrosystem is in ecological systems theory, the cultural values, laws and customs that surround a child.
The microsystem is in ecological systems theory, the groups that have direct contact with the child, such as family and school.
The mesosystem is in ecological systems theory, the relationships between the groups in a child's immediate surroundings.
The exosystem is in ecological systems theory, the settings that affect a child indirectly, such as a parent's workplace.

questions.explanation: The macrosystem is in ecological systems theory, the cultural values, laws and customs that surround a child.

questions.stem: Without knowing any of them, Mr. Hill feels dislike and distrust toward people from a neighboring town. This feeling is an example of which of the following?

options.why: Correct. Prejudice is an unjustified negative attitude toward a group and its members.
A stereotype is a generalized belief about a group of people.
The just-world phenomenon is the tendency to believe that people get what they deserve.
Discrimination is unjustified negative behavior toward a group and its members.

questions.explanation: Prejudice is an unjustified negative attitude toward a group and its members.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a taste aversion?

options.text: Learning that happens after a single pairing of two stimuli
options.why: That describes one-trial conditioning.

options.text: The replacing of an unwanted response to a stimulus with a new response, by pairing the stimulus with something pleasant
options.why: That describes counterconditioning.

options.text: A learned dislike of a food that was followed by illness
options.why: Correct. This is what a taste aversion means.

options.text: The inborn readiness to learn some associations, such as taste and nausea, more easily than others
options.why: That describes biological preparedness.

questions.explanation: A taste aversion is a learned dislike of a food that was followed by illness.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes homeostasis?

options.text: The body's tendency to keep its internal state, such as temperature, steady
options.why: Correct. This is what homeostasis means.

options.text: The theory that behavior is pulled by rewards from outside the person
options.why: That describes incentive theory.

options.text: The theory that behavior is driven by fixed, inborn patterns that are not learned
options.why: That describes instinct theory.

options.text: The principle that performance is best at a moderate level of arousal
options.why: That describes the Yerkes-Dodson law.

questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the body's tendency to keep its internal state, such as temperature, steady.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the Gestalt principle that we fill in gaps to see a complete, whole object?

options.why: Proximity is the Gestalt principle that we group together objects that are near each other.
Similarity is the Gestalt principle that we group together objects that look alike.
Figure and ground is the Gestalt principle that we organize a scene into an object that stands out and its background.
Correct. Closure is the Gestalt principle that we fill in gaps to see a complete, whole object.

questions.explanation: Closure is the Gestalt principle that we fill in gaps to see a complete, whole object.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as a state of heightened suggestibility that can help reduce pain and anxiety but does not reliably recover memories?

options.why: Person-centered therapy is the humanistic therapy in which the therapist provides acceptance and empathy so that the client can grow.
Active listening is the technique of echoing, restating and seeking clarification of what the client says.
Correct. Hypnosis is a state of heightened suggestibility that can help reduce pain and anxiety but does not reliably recover memories.
Free association is the psychodynamic technique in which the client says whatever comes to mind.

questions.explanation: Hypnosis is a state of heightened suggestibility that can help reduce pain and anxiety but does not reliably recover memories.

questions.stem: What is the independent variable in this study?

options.why: This was measured, not manipulated: it is the dependent variable.
This is a procedure for forming the groups, not a variable.
Correct. The independent variable is the factor the researchers changed between the two conditions.

options.text: The number of participants in the study
options.why: This is the sample size, not a variable the researchers changed.

questions.explanation: The independent variable is the factor the researchers changed between the two conditions.

questions.stem: Dana pictures the layout of her house to count the windows. Which part of working memory is she using?

options.why: Long-term potentiation is the strengthening of the connections between neurons after repeated activation, which is the biological basis of memory.
The phonological loop is the part of working memory that briefly holds spoken and written words.
The central executive is the part of working memory that directs attention and coordinates the other parts.
Correct. The visuospatial sketchpad is the part of working memory that briefly holds images and spatial information.

questions.explanation: The visuospatial sketchpad is the part of working memory that briefly holds images and spatial information.

questions.stem: In one culture, wearing skirts is considered masculine; in another, it is considered feminine. This difference best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Correct. Gender is the socially and culturally influenced attitudes, feelings and behaviors that a culture links to being a boy, girl, man or woman.
Sexual orientation is the direction of a person's enduring sexual attraction.
A gender role is the set of behaviors that a culture expects of men or of women.
Sex is the biological characteristics, such as chromosomes and anatomy, by which people are classified as male, female or intersex.

questions.explanation: Gender is the socially and culturally influenced attitudes, feelings and behaviors that a culture links to being a boy, girl, man or woman.

questions.stem: A sleeper's EEG shows large, slow delta waves, and she is very difficult to wake. Which stage of sleep is she in?

options.why: REM rebound is the tendency to have more REM sleep after being deprived of it.
The circadian rhythm is the body's roughly 24-hour cycle of wakefulness and sleep.
Correct. NREM stage 3 is the deep sleep stage marked by slow delta waves, in which a person is hard to wake.
NREM stage 1 is the brief, light first stage of sleep, in which a person may have hypnagogic sensations such as falling.

questions.explanation: NREM stage 3 is the deep sleep stage marked by slow delta waves, in which a person is hard to wake.

questions.stem: Students are asked whether each word on a list would fit in a sentence about cooking, and they later remember these words best. Which level of processing does this task use?

options.why: Effortful processing is the encoding that requires attention and conscious effort.
Explicit memory is the memory of facts and experiences that a person can consciously recall and state.
Correct. Semantic encoding is the deep encoding of a word based on its meaning.
Automatic processing is the encoding of information, such as space, time and frequency, without conscious effort.

questions.explanation: Semantic encoding is the deep encoding of a word based on its meaning.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes stigma?

options.text: The American Psychiatric Association's manual for classifying and diagnosing psychological disorders
options.why: That describes the DSM.

options.text: The criterion for a disorder that the behavior differs markedly from what a culture expects
options.why: That describes deviation from the social norm.

options.text: The negative attitudes and discrimination directed at people who have a psychological disorder
options.why: Correct. This is what stigma means.

options.text: The criterion for a disorder that the behavior causes suffering to the person
options.why: That describes distress.

questions.explanation: Stigma is the negative attitudes and discrimination directed at people who have a psychological disorder.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as perception that is guided by experience, expectations and context?

options.why: Correct. Top-down processing is perception that is guided by experience, expectations and context.
Inattentional blindness is the failure to notice a visible object because attention is directed elsewhere.
The cocktail party effect is the ability to notice personally important information, such as your name, in an unattended conversation.
Selective attention is the focusing of awareness on one stimulus while ignoring others.

questions.explanation: Top-down processing is perception that is guided by experience, expectations and context.

questions.stem: Why is this study not an experiment?

options.why: Experiments also test hypotheses.
Experiments also use numerical data.

options.text: The researchers did not manipulate a variable or randomly assign anyone to conditions
options.why: Correct. An experiment requires a manipulated independent variable and random assignment.
Sample size does not determine the research method.

questions.explanation: An experiment requires a manipulated independent variable and random assignment.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the operational definition of the dependent variable?

options.text: The random assignment of each one to a condition
options.why: This is a control procedure, not a definition of a variable.
This names the variable but does not say how it was measured.

options.text: The percentage of homeowners in each group who agreed to display the sign
options.why: Correct. An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

options.text: Whether a small request came first
options.why: This is the independent variable.

questions.explanation: An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

questions.stem: The participants who were with other people took longer to report the smoke. The difference was statistically significant. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The hypothesis has been proved, so the study need not be repeated
options.why: Findings must be replicated; one study does not prove a hypothesis.

options.text: The number of other people present and the reporting of an emergency are related, but no cause can be inferred
options.why: That limit applies to correlational studies; this was an experiment.

options.text: The same result would be found in every group of people or animals
options.why: The sample limits how far the result can be generalized.

options.text: The number of other people present caused the difference in the reporting of an emergency
options.why: Correct. With random assignment and a manipulated variable, an experiment supports a conclusion about cause and effect.

questions.explanation: With random assignment and a manipulated variable, an experiment supports a conclusion about cause and effect.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Wernicke's area?

options.text: The arrangement in which each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body
options.why: That describes contralateral control.

options.text: The area in the left temporal lobe that controls language comprehension
options.why: Correct. This is what Wernicke's area means.

options.text: The area in the left frontal lobe that controls speech production
options.why: That describes Broca's area.

options.text: The tendency for each side of the brain to handle certain functions, such as language in the left hemisphere
options.why: That describes hemispheric specialization.

questions.explanation: Wernicke's area is the area in the left temporal lobe that controls language comprehension.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a possible third variable that could explain the correlation?

options.text: The number of days of illness in a year
options.why: This is one of the two variables that were measured.
This is the statistic, not a variable.
This is one of the two variables that were measured.
Correct. A third variable could influence both measures and so produce the correlation.

questions.explanation: A third variable could influence both measures and so produce the correlation.

questions.stem: A three-year-old says that the moon is following her and that her teddy bear is sad. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Correct. Animism is the belief of young children that lifeless objects have feelings and intentions.
Reversibility is the understanding that an action can be undone to return things to their original state.
Object permanence is the understanding that things continue to exist when they are out of sight.
Theory of mind is the understanding that other people have their own thoughts, beliefs and feelings.

questions.explanation: Animism is the belief of young children that lifeless objects have feelings and intentions.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes executive functions?

options.text: The tendency to approach a problem in a way that has worked before, even when it no longer works
options.why: That describes a mental set.

options.text: The mental processes used to plan, organize and carry out goal-directed behavior
options.why: Correct. This is what executive functions means.

options.text: A step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution
options.why: That describes an algorithm.

options.text: The inability to see that an object can be used for something other than its usual purpose
options.why: That describes functional fixedness.

questions.explanation: Executive functions is the mental processes used to plan, organize and carry out goal-directed behavior.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the spacing effect?

options.text: The tendency to remember the last items in a list well
options.why: That describes the recency effect.

options.text: The tendency to remember the first and last items in a list better than the middle ones
options.why: That describes the serial position effect.

options.text: The tendency to remember the first items in a list well
options.why: That describes the primacy effect.

options.text: The finding that study spread over time produces better long-term memory than study crammed together
options.why: Correct. This is what the spacing effect means.

questions.explanation: The spacing effect is the finding that study spread over time produces better long-term memory than study crammed together.

questions.stem: A vending machine delivers a snack every time money is inserted. Which schedule of reinforcement is this?

options.why: Correct. Continuous reinforcement is the schedule in which the behavior is reinforced every time it occurs.
A fixed-interval schedule is the schedule in which the first response after a set amount of time is reinforced.
A variable-interval schedule is the schedule in which the first response after an unpredictable amount of time is reinforced.
A variable-ratio schedule is the schedule in which the behavior is reinforced after an unpredictable number of responses.

questions.explanation: Continuous reinforcement is the schedule in which the behavior is reinforced every time it occurs.

questions.stem: A child gets out of bed during deep sleep, walks to the kitchen, and remembers nothing in the morning. Which sleep disorder is this?

options.why: Correct. Somnambulism is sleepwalking, which occurs during deep NREM sleep.
Insomnia is a sleep disorder with ongoing difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep.
REM sleep behavior disorder is a sleep disorder in which the normal paralysis of REM sleep is missing, so the person acts out dreams.
Sleep apnea is a sleep disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops during sleep, causing brief awakenings.

questions.explanation: Somnambulism is sleepwalking, which occurs during deep NREM sleep.

questions.stem: Asked to think of a bird, most people picture a robin rather than a penguin. The robin is serving as which of the following?

options.why: Accommodation is the changing of an existing schema to fit new information.
Assimilation is the interpretation of a new experience in terms of an existing schema.
A concept is a mental grouping of similar objects, events, ideas or people.
Correct. A prototype is the best or most typical example of a category.

questions.explanation: A prototype is the best or most typical example of a category.

questions.stem: Over several years, a young man slowly becomes more withdrawn and odd, and his symptoms persist for decades. Which pattern is this?

options.why: Correct. A chronic course is the slow, gradual development of schizophrenia, from which recovery is less likely.
An acute onset is the sudden appearance of schizophrenia, often after stress, from which recovery is more likely.
A negative symptom is a symptom of schizophrenia that takes away a normal behavior, such as emotional expression or motivation.
A positive symptom is a symptom of schizophrenia that adds an inappropriate behavior or experience, such as hallucinations.

questions.explanation: A chronic course is the slow, gradual development of schizophrenia, from which recovery is less likely.

questions.stem: A psychologist notes that people who score high on verbal tests also tend to score high on spatial and numerical tests, and concludes that one ability underlies them all. Which idea is this?

options.why: Correct. General intelligence is the single underlying mental ability that Spearman believed affects performance on all mental tasks.
Multiple intelligences is the theory that people have several independent kinds of intelligence, such as musical and interpersonal.
The Flynn effect is the steady rise in average intelligence test scores over the generations.
Mental age is the level of performance typical of a certain chronological age on an intelligence test.

questions.explanation: General intelligence is the single underlying mental ability that Spearman believed affects performance on all mental tasks.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the operational definition of the dependent variable?

options.why: This names the variable but does not say how it was measured.
This is the independent variable.

options.text: The random assignment of each one to a condition
options.why: This is a control procedure, not a definition of a variable.

options.text: The number of new puzzles out of ten that each child later solved without help
options.why: Correct. An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

questions.explanation: An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

questions.stem: Can the researchers conclude that resting heart rate causes a change in self-rated anxiety?

options.text: No, because a correlation does not show cause and effect
options.why: Correct. Without manipulating a variable and assigning subjects at random, other explanations cannot be ruled out.

options.text: No, because correlations can only be calculated in experiments
options.why: Correlations are calculated in non-experimental studies.

options.text: Yes, because the correlation is not zero
options.why: Any nonzero correlation still leaves the cause unknown.

options.text: Yes, because the sample was large
options.why: A large sample does not turn a correlation into evidence of causation.

questions.explanation: Without manipulating a variable and assigning subjects at random, other explanations cannot be ruled out.

questions.stem: Jon feels dissatisfied with his running times after comparing himself with the fastest runner on the team. Which process is this?

options.why: Correct. Upward social comparison is the comparing of oneself with people who are doing better.
The mere exposure effect is the tendency to like something more simply because we have encountered it repeatedly.
A dispositional attribution is an explanation of behavior that points to the person's own traits or character.
A situational attribution is an explanation of behavior that points to outside circumstances.

questions.explanation: Upward social comparison is the comparing of oneself with people who are doing better.

questions.stem: Neurotransmitters must cross a small space to reach the next neuron. What is this space called?

options.why: The axon is the long fiber that carries the neural impulse away from the cell body toward other cells.
The axon terminals is the endings of the axon that release neurotransmitters.
Correct. The synapse is the tiny gap between the sending neuron and the receiving neuron.
The myelin sheath is the fatty layer around some axons that speeds up neural impulses.

questions.explanation: The synapse is the tiny gap between the sending neuron and the receiving neuron.

questions.stem: After a stroke, other areas of Sara's brain gradually take over the lost function. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: A split brain is the condition in which the two hemispheres cannot communicate because the corpus callosum has been cut.
An EEG is a recording of the electrical waves that sweep across the brain's surface.
Correct. Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change by reorganizing after damage or building new pathways through experience.
A case study is an in-depth study of one individual, such as a patient with unusual brain damage.

questions.explanation: Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change by reorganizing after damage or building new pathways through experience.

questions.stem: 'Because I said so' is the only explanation that Tara's parents ever give for their many strict rules. Which parenting style is this?

options.why: Authoritative parenting is the parenting style that sets firm rules but explains them, listens and is warm.
Correct. Authoritarian parenting is the parenting style that sets strict rules and expects obedience, with little warmth or discussion.
Temperament is a person's characteristic emotional reactivity and intensity, which appears early in life.
Permissive parenting is the parenting style that makes few demands and sets few limits.

questions.explanation: Authoritarian parenting is the parenting style that sets strict rules and expects obedience, with little warmth or discussion.

questions.stem: After being paid only one dollar to tell others that a boring task was fun, students came to believe the task really was enjoyable. Which concept best explains this change of attitude?

options.why: Correct. Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort a person feels when their actions and attitudes conflict, which motivates a change in one of them.
Belief perseverance is the tendency to hold on to a belief even after the evidence for it has been discredited.
Out-group homogeneity bias is the tendency to see the members of other groups as all alike.
In-group bias is the tendency to favor the members of one's own group.

questions.explanation: Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort a person feels when their actions and attitudes conflict, which motivates a change in one of them.

questions.stem: After a high test score, Sue says she is clever; after a low score, she says the test was unfair. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Correct. The self-serving bias is the tendency to credit our successes to ourselves and blame our failures on outside factors.
Relative deprivation is the feeling of being worse off than the people one compares oneself with.
An optimistic explanatory style is the habit of explaining bad events as temporary, specific and caused by outside factors.
A pessimistic explanatory style is the habit of explaining bad events as lasting, affecting everything and caused by oneself.

questions.explanation: The self-serving bias is the tendency to credit our successes to ourselves and blame our failures on outside factors.

questions.stem: Teenagers often act on impulse partly because the brain area for planning and self-control is still maturing. Which area is this?

options.why: Correct. The prefrontal cortex is the front part of the frontal lobes, which handles executive functions such as planning and self-control.
The frontal lobes is the lobes behind the forehead, which handle planning, judgment and voluntary movement.
The occipital lobes is the lobes at the back of the head, which process visual information.
The somatosensory cortex is the strip at the front of the parietal lobes that registers touch and body sensations.

questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex is the front part of the frontal lobes, which handles executive functions such as planning and self-control.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes unconditional positive regard?

options.text: In psychodynamic theory, the store of thoughts, wishes and memories that a person is not aware of but that still influences behavior
options.why: That describes the unconscious.

options.text: In psychodynamic theory, a method the ego uses without awareness to reduce anxiety by distorting reality
options.why: That describes a defense mechanism.

options.text: A personality test, such as an inkblot test, that asks people to interpret unclear images in order to reveal hidden feelings
options.why: That describes a projective test.

options.text: The attitude of total acceptance toward another person, whatever they say or do
options.why: Correct. This is what unconditional positive regard means.

questions.explanation: Unconditional positive regard is the attitude of total acceptance toward another person, whatever they say or do.

questions.stem: In elevators, people face the door and avoid staring at strangers, although no law requires it. This unwritten rule is an example of which of the following?

options.why: The central route to persuasion is persuasion that works through evidence and logical arguments, which people think about carefully.
Correct. A social norm is a rule for accepted and expected behavior in a group.
Informational social influence is the influence that comes from a person's willingness to accept others' views as evidence about reality.
The halo effect is the tendency for one good quality of a person to make us assume they have other good qualities.

questions.explanation: A social norm is a rule for accepted and expected behavior in a group.

questions.stem: Kim knows that Paris is the capital of France, although she cannot remember when she learned it. Which kind of memory is this?

options.why: Episodic memory is the explicit memory of personally experienced events.
Procedural memory is the implicit memory of how to perform skills and actions.
Prospective memory is the memory to carry out a planned action in the future.
Correct. Semantic memory is the explicit memory of facts and general knowledge.

questions.explanation: Semantic memory is the explicit memory of facts and general knowledge.

questions.title: Article analysis: a study of attention to the road

parts.prompt: Identify the research method used in the study.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the method as an experiment.
rubric.example: The study is an experiment: the researchers manipulated a variable and randomly assigned the subjects to conditions.

parts.prompt: State the operational definition of attention to the road.

rubric.criterion: States how the variable was measured in this study.
rubric.example: Attention to the road was defined as the number of road signs out of 30 that each participant failed to notice.

parts.prompt: Describe the meaning of the difference between the two group averages.

rubric.criterion: Accurately describes which group scored higher or lower and what that means for the variable measured.
rubric.example: The phone group missed more road signs. On average, the value was 11.4 for the group that talked on the phone and 4.9 for the group that drove without a phone, and a p value of 0.01 means a difference this large is unlikely to be due to chance.

parts.prompt: Identify at least one ethical guideline applied by the researchers.

rubric.criterion: Identifies an ethical guideline that the summary shows was followed.
rubric.example: Informed consent: participants agreed to take part after being told about the study. (Also acceptable: debriefing; the right to withdraw; approval by an institutional review board.)

parts.prompt: Explain the extent to which the research findings may or may not be generalizable, using specific and relevant evidence from the study.

rubric.criterion: Explains a limit (or strength) of generalizability with reference to the sample.
rubric.example: The sample was 64 licensed drivers from one city, so the findings may not apply to people of other ages, cultures or backgrounds. Because the sample was not randomly selected from a wider population, it may not be representative.

parts.prompt: Explain how at least one of the research findings supports or refutes the researchers' hypothesis.

rubric.criterion: Uses a specific finding from the study as evidence.
rubric.example: The phone group missed more road signs. (11.4 compared with 4.9).

rubric.criterion: Explains how the finding supports the hypothesis, using a psychological concept.
rubric.example: This supports the hypothesis that phone use affects attention to the road. Because subjects were randomly assigned, the difference can be attributed to phone use. The finding illustrates selective attention and inattentional blindness: attention is limited, so people fail to notice visible objects when attention is elsewhere.

questions.title: Evidence-based question: Do rewards increase motivation?

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim, based in psychological science, that responds to the question.

rubric.criterion: States a claim that answers the question and can be supported by the sources.
rubric.example: Rewards increase a behavior while they last, but they can reduce intrinsic motivation, so the behavior falls when the rewards stop.

parts.prompt: (i) Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources. (ii) Explain how the evidence supports your claim, using a psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP Psychology.

rubric.criterion: Uses specific, relevant evidence from one source and names the source.
rubric.example: In Source A, children promised a certificate later chose to draw for 6.5 minutes, compared with 13.8 minutes for children who were not rewarded.

rubric.criterion: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
rubric.example: This supports the claim through intrinsic and extrinsic motivation: the reward gave the children an external reason for drawing, which weakened their desire to draw for its own sake.

rubric.criterion: Correctly applies a psychological concept in the explanation.
rubric.example: The concept must be named and applied correctly, as in the model explanation.

parts.prompt: (i) Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source. (ii) Explain how this evidence supports your claim, using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding.

rubric.criterion: Uses specific, relevant evidence from a different source and names the source.
rubric.example: In Source B, workers paid a bonus made more sales (41 compared with 33), but their sales fell to 30 when the bonus ended.

rubric.criterion: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
rubric.example: This supports the claim through operant conditioning: the bonus acted as positive reinforcement, which increased the behavior, and when reinforcement stopped the behavior declined (extinction).

rubric.criterion: Correctly applies a different psychological concept from the one used in part B.
rubric.example: The concept must differ from the one used in part B and be applied correctly.
